raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old male patient (63 kg, 180 cm) visited our hospital for an anal condyloma. Excisional biopsy under spinal anesthesia was scheduled. On preoperative examination, the blood test showed positive for HIV antibodies. Thus, a lymphocyte subset test was performed, and the patient was diagnosed with HIV based on the following results: CD4(+) T-cells 324/mul, CD4 14.2% (28.4-56.4), and CD4/CD8 0.2 (0.9 - 3.6). There was no record of particular significance in the patient's past medical history. His blood test showed following: Hemoglobin 15.8 g/dl, hematocrit 45.7%, and platelet 217,000 cell/mm3. The patient's blood coagulation was also in the normal range with a prothrombin time (PT) of 13.5 s (INR 1.3) and an activated partial thromboplastin time of 35.7 s. His chest X-ray and electrocardiograph findings were also normal.
Without premedication, on arriving at the operating room, the patient's vital signs read as follows: Blood pressure (BP) 147/66 mmHg, pulse 70 beats/min, and O2 saturation 100%.
Spinal anesthesia was performed in sitting position with midline approach at L3-4 space, using a 25-gauge, Quincke (Hakko Co. Ltd, Chikuma, Japan) needle. The drug used 8 mg of 0.5% bupivacaine (Marcaine , AstraZeneca) was administered successfully in the first attempt. His vital signs were stable. The operation was concluded in 35 min without any abnormal findings. After 4 h, the patient started to experience a headache without nausea and vomiting in the general ward.
The symptom was not related to the position. A headache improved partially following bed rest and taking 650 mg of acetaminophen (Tylenol ER ). The patient was discharged 1 day after the surgery with no abnormal symptoms.
One day after the discharge, the patient experienced a headache with accompanying nausea and vomiting. The patient visited the emergency room after a headache had aggravated further. BP was 150/81 mmHg, and pulse was 95 beats/min at the time. There were no neurologic anomalies found during the physical exam. He was hospitalized at the neurology department for further evaluation and conservative management.
On the 1st day, the patient's headache did not improve despite fluid management, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and bed rest. We performed an enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging to identify the cause of a headache and found a small amount of SDH in the left occipital region and interhemispheric fissure [Figure 1].
On the 2nd day, an epidural blood patch (EBP) was performed because the patient's symptoms still did not improve. A 20-gauge Tuohy needle (Portex , Smiths Medical) was used to administer 10 ml of autologous blood through an L3-4 epidural space. After EBP, a headache (numeric rating scale, level 6) regardless of the patient's posture was continued. After that, a headache improved gradually following bed rest and hydration.
On the 7th day, a computed tomography scan was performed; the amount of SDH decreased, and there were no other abnormal organic findings that may have induced headache [Figure 2]. The patient was discharged because his headache was mitigated with no other neurologic symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presented for excisional biopsy of perianal condylomata and subsequently returned to the emergency room on postoperative day 2 with a severe, non-positional headache accompanied by nausea and vomiting after spinal anesthesia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Scheduled for excisional biopsy of anal condyloma under spinal anesthesia (25-gauge Quincke needle at L3–L4 with 8 mg of 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine), the patient tested positive for HIV on routine preoperative screening. Four hours postoperatively, he developed a non-postural headache that partially responded to bed rest and acetaminophen (650 mg), allowing discharge on postoperative day 1. On postoperative day 2, his headache severely worsened with nausea and vomiting, remained refractory to IV fluids, NSAIDs, and an L3–L4 autologous epidural blood patch (10 mL), and prompted brain MRI evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Perianal condyloma acuminata; newly diagnosed HIV infection on preoperative screening; otherwise unremarkable past medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive postoperatively for severe non-positional headache (NRS 6/10), nausea, and vomiting; negative for focal neurological deficits.

objective.physical_examination: Height 180 cm, weight 63 kg. Preoperative vitals: BP 147/66 mmHg, pulse 70 beats/min, SpO2 100%. Emergency room readmission vitals (postoperative day 2): BP 150/81 mmHg, pulse 95 beats/min, with a completely normal neurological examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Preoperative labs showed positive HIV antibody screening, hemoglobin 15.8 g/dL, hematocrit 45.7%, platelets 217,000/mm3, PT 13.5 s (INR 1.3), and aPTT 35.7 s. Preoperative chest X-ray and ECG were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Preoperative lymphocyte subset analysis confirmed HIV-related immunodeficiency: CD4+ T-cell count 324/µL, CD4% 14.2% (reference 28.4–56.4%), and CD4/CD8 ratio 0.2 (reference 0.9–3.6). Contrast-enhanced brain MRI on readmission day 1 demonstrated a small intracranial subdural hematoma (SDH) in the left occipital convexity and interhemispheric fissure; follow-up head CT on hospital day 7 showed regression of the subdural hematoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Intracranial subdural hematoma (left occipital and interhemispheric fissure) following dural puncture for spinal anesthesia (25G Quincke needle) in a 25-year-old male with newly diagnosed HIV infection (CD4+ count 324/µL [14.2%], CD4/CD8 ratio 0.2) undergoing anal condyloma excision. Note that an autologous epidural blood patch (10 mL at L3–L4) was performed on hospital day 2 without immediate postural relief; with conservative inpatient management (bed rest, hydration, and analgesia), the subdural hematoma regressed on day 7 head CT and the patient was discharged headache-free without neurological sequelae.
